mcqs.question: Why does `copy.items.add("banana")` also change `original.items` in the shallow-copy example?
options: Because add() on a List always mutates every Cart in scope
Because Cart's shallowCopy() passes the same list reference to both objects, so they point at one shared list
Because Java automatically synchronizes all List fields across object copies
mcqs.explanation: shallowCopy() hands the new Cart the exact same list reference, so both objects' items field points at one underlying list — mutating it through either reference is visible through both. There's no automatic synchronization and equals() has nothing to do with this.

mcqs.question: Per the diagram, what's the structural difference between the shallow-copy and deep-copy pictures?
options: The deep copy has more fields than the shallow copy
The shallow copy runs faster at the cost of using more memory
In the shallow copy, both Cart objects point at one shared items list; in the deep copy, each Cart points at its own independent list
The shallow copy diagram shows only one Cart object total
mcqs.explanation: The diagram's core point is reference sharing versus independence — same field structure in both cases, but shallow shares one list while deep gives each Cart its own. Shallow copy typically uses less memory, not more, and both diagrams show two Cart objects.

mcqs.question: Why does the deep-vs-shallow copy distinction disappear when every field of a class is immutable?
options: Because immutable classes cannot be copied at all
Because Java automatically deep-copies immutable classes behind the scenes
Because immutable classes don't support the clone() method
Because there's no mutable state left that could leak between the original and the copy, so sharing references is exactly as safe as duplicating them
mcqs.explanation: With no mutable state, reference-sharing and duplication are behaviorally identical, so the distinction becomes moot. Immutable classes can be copied and can implement clone() like any other class — nothing automatic happens behind the scenes.

mcqs.question: Why is assuming Java's Object.clone() (or a C++ default copy constructor) performs a deep copy a wrong assumption?
options: Because these mechanisms are shallow by default — they copy references to nested mutable objects, not the objects themselves, unless you explicitly implement deep copying
Because clone() always throws an exception unless overridden
Because C++ doesn't have copy constructors at all
Because deep copying is only possible using external serialization libraries
mcqs.explanation: Both mechanisms copy field values, which for reference-typed fields means copying the reference, not the referenced object — that's shallow by default. clone() doesn't always throw, C++ absolutely has copy constructors, and deep copying can be implemented directly without any external library.
